Decision-making that is rational within the real limits of information, cognitive capacity, and time.
Choosing the first alternative that meets an acceptable threshold rather than searching for the optimal option.
Overweighting information that is easily recalled or recently encountered.
Seeking out and favoring information that confirms existing beliefs while discounting contradictory evidence.
An initial piece of information exerting disproportionate influence on subsequent judgments.

practice.q: Bounded rationality describes decision-making that is:
choices: Rational within the real limits of available information, cognitive capacity, and time
Completely irrational and random
Only possible for artificial intelligence systems
Identical to the idealized rational decision-making model
practice.explain: Bounded rationality acknowledges real-world limits that the idealized rational model ignores.

practice.q: Satisficing refers to:
choices: Choosing the first alternative that meets an acceptable threshold rather than searching for the single optimal option
Always selecting the cheapest available option
A decision made with zero criteria of any kind
An approach used only by inexperienced managers
practice.explain: Satisficing accepts a good-enough option rather than exhaustively searching for the single best one.

practice.q: A manager who judges every job candidate against the very first candidate she interviewed, regardless of that first candidate's actual qualifications, is likely exhibiting:
choices: Anchoring bias
Confirmation bias
Availability bias
No bias at all, since comparison is always objective
practice.explain: Letting an initial reference point disproportionately shape later judgments is the hallmark of anchoring bias.

lessons.title: Innovation and Entrepreneurship in Established Firms
lessons.intro: Large, successful companies are often better at optimizing what already works than at inventing what's next, which is exactly why so many established firms deliberately build internal structures whose entire job is to act more like a scrappy startup.

sections.heading: Innovation in Established Organizations
body: **Innovation** is the process of translating a new idea into a product, service, or process that creates value, distinct from **invention**, which is simply the creation of something new regardless of whether it ever finds practical, valuable application. Established companies often innovate incrementally, improving existing products steadily, since incremental innovation carries lower risk and fits more easily within existing processes, budgets, and reporting structures.

**Disruptive innovation**, a term describing a new product or business model that initially serves an overlooked or underserved market segment with a simpler, cheaper offering, then gradually improves to seriously threaten established competitors' core markets, is notoriously difficult for large incumbent firms to respond to, since it often looks unattractive and unprofitable by their existing standards until it's already gained real, hard-to-dislodge momentum.

sections.heading: Intrapreneurship
body: **Intrapreneurship** applies entrepreneurial thinking, risk-taking, resourcefulness, and a willingness to challenge existing assumptions, within an established organization rather than through founding an independent new venture. Companies encourage intrapreneurship through dedicated innovation labs, protected time for employees to pursue new ideas, such as a fixed percentage of work hours, and internal funding mechanisms that operate somewhat like an internal venture capital process.

Intrapreneurship faces a structural tension unique to established organizations: it requires tolerating a level of failure and uncertainty that runs directly against the efficiency-focused, predictable metrics most established organizations use to reward managers elsewhere in the business, which is why successful intrapreneurship programs often deliberately shield new initiatives from the company's normal short-term performance metrics, at least for a defined period.

sections.heading: Building a Culture That Supports Innovation
body: Organizations that sustain innovation over time typically tolerate calculated, well-reasoned failure as a natural cost of genuine experimentation, rather than punishing every failed initiative as harshly as they would punish simple operational negligence — a culture that punishes all failure equally teaches employees to avoid any real risk-taking altogether, quietly strangling the exact experimentation innovation actually requires.

Cross-functional collaboration is also a common ingredient: many genuinely valuable innovations emerge at the intersection of two previously separate departments' knowledge, such as engineering and customer service jointly identifying a product flaw that neither department alone would have fully understood or prioritized fixing.

example.problem: A well-established camera company dismisses an early, lower-quality digital camera prototype as unprofitable and inferior to its core film camera business, and declines to invest further. Using the concept of disruptive innovation, explain why this decision, though reasonable by the company's existing standards, might prove costly.
steps: Recognize the pattern: an initially inferior, cheaper alternative that doesn't yet threaten the core market by existing performance standards is the classic profile of disruptive innovation.

Note that disruptive innovations typically improve over time along a trajectory the established leader initially underestimates, since it looks unprofitable by their existing standards at the earlier stage.

Conclude that dismissing the technology using existing performance and profitability metrics is a reasonable short-term decision that nonetheless risks missing the long-term disruptive threat, a well-documented historical pattern in exactly this kind of established-industry disruption.
example.answer: This decision follows the classic disruptive innovation pattern — the new technology looks unprofitable and inferior by current standards, but if it improves along its own trajectory, it can eventually threaten the established company's core market, a risk the existing evaluation standards are poorly suited to detect early.

keyTerms.def: The process of translating a new idea into a product, service, or process that creates value.
The creation of something new, regardless of whether it finds practical, valuable application.
A new, initially simpler and cheaper offering that improves over time to threaten established competitors' core markets.
Applying entrepreneurial thinking and risk-taking within an established organization.
Steady, lower-risk improvement of existing products or processes.

practice.q: Innovation differs from invention in that innovation:
choices: Translates a new idea into a product, service, or process that actually creates value
Is identical to invention in every respect
Only applies to new physical products, never services
Requires no new idea whatsoever
practice.explain: Innovation requires translating an idea into practical value, unlike invention, which is simply creating something new.

practice.q: Disruptive innovation is difficult for established firms to respond to primarily because:
choices: It initially looks unattractive and unprofitable by the firm's existing standards until it gains real momentum
Established firms are legally prohibited from responding to it
It always fails completely and never threatens existing markets
It requires no investment of any kind to counter
practice.explain: Disruptive innovations look unprofitable early on by incumbent standards, delaying a serious response until it's harder to counter.

practice.q: Intrapreneurship refers to:
choices: Applying entrepreneurial thinking and risk-taking within an established organization
Founding an entirely independent new company
A synonym for incremental innovation only
A process that requires no organizational support of any kind
practice.explain: Intrapreneurship applies startup-style thinking inside an existing, established organization.
